questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Scale signal to noise with exposure
questions.stem: A 1-hour exposure reaches SNR 10; a 82-hour exposure reaches about:

options.misconception: assumes signal to noise grows linearly
adds exposure time to the ratio
inverts the square-root scaling

questions.explanation: For photon noise, signal to noise grows as the square root of exposure time, so 82 hours gives about 90.6. Four times the time doubles the ratio.
questions.hint: Signal to noise improves as the square root of time.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star counted at 595 photons/s versus a reference at 1000 photons/s is fainter by how many magnitudes?

options.misconception: uses the raw count ratio as magnitudes
multiplies the ratio by 2.5
halves the logarithmic coefficient

questions.explanation: Magnitude difference is 2.5 times log of the reference count over the target count, about 0.56. The magnitude scale compresses large flux ratios.
questions.hint: Use 2.5 times the base-ten logarithm.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An interferometer with baseline 810 m at 500 nm resolves about how many milliarcseconds?

options.misconception: doubles the angular resolution
halves the angular resolution
uses the baseline as an angle

questions.explanation: Angular resolution is wavelength over baseline, about 0.13 milliarcseconds here. Longer baselines resolve far finer detail than a single dish.
questions.hint: Resolution improves as the baseline grows.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Two independent errors of 1 and 11 combine in quadrature to about:

options.misconception: adds errors linearly
multiplies the errors
keeps only the larger error

questions.explanation: Independent uncertainties add in quadrature, the square root of 1 squared plus 11 squared, about 11.05. Linear addition overstates the combined error.
questions.hint: Square, add, then take the square root.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A photon of wavelength 740 nm has energy about how many electronvolts?

options.misconception: inverts the wavelength relation
multiplies by the conversion constant
halves the photon energy

questions.explanation: Photon energy in electronvolts is 1240 divided by wavelength in nanometers, about 1.68 eV here. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon.
questions.hint: Energy and wavelength are inversely related.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An object spans 41.5 arcminutes on the sky; its angular size in degrees is:

options.misconception: treats arcminutes as if they were degrees
uses arcseconds per degree by mistake
multiplies by sixty instead of dividing

questions.explanation: There are 60 arcminutes in one degree, so dividing 41.5 by 60 gives 0.692 degrees. Treating arcminutes as degrees skips that conversion entirely.
questions.hint: A degree contains 60 arcminutes.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Star A at magnitude 17 outshines star B at magnitude 19 by what factor?

options.misconception: uses the magnitude difference itself as a factor
treats each magnitude as a factor of one hundred
halves the magnitude step before exponentiating

questions.explanation: A difference of 2 magnitudes corresponds to 2.512 raised to 2, about 6.31 times brighter. The magnitude difference alone is logarithmic, not a brightness ratio.
questions.hint: Each five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star has a parallax of 42.5 milliarcseconds; its distance in parsecs is:

options.misconception: mistakes the parallax angle for the distance
multiplies the angle by 1000 instead of dividing
divides by parallax twice

questions.explanation: Distance in parsecs equals 1000 divided by parallax in milliarcseconds, giving 23.53 pc. Parallax is a small angle and shrinks as the star gets farther away.
questions.hint: One parsec is the distance with one arcsecond of parallax.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star rises at 7:21 tonight; about how many minutes earlier will it rise tomorrow night?

options.misconception: confuses the 24-hour solar day with the shift
uses a full hour as the nightly advance
assumes stars rise at the same clock time

questions.explanation: A sidereal day is roughly four minutes shorter than a solar day, so a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. That is why constellations drift through the seasons.
questions.hint: The sidereal day is about 23h 56m.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: When the Moon is 214 degrees from the Sun, the illuminated fraction is about:

options.misconception: uses the wrong sign for the cosine term
takes the angle fraction as the lit fraction
forgets to halve the geometric factor

questions.explanation: The sunlit fraction of the lunar disk is (1 minus cos of the elongation) over 2, which gives 0.91 here. At full moon the elongation is 180 degrees and the fraction reaches one.
questions.hint: Full moon means an elongation of 180 degrees.

questions.stem: A star at declination +82 degrees lies how many degrees north of the celestial equator?

options.misconception: uses the complement to the pole instead
doubles the declination value
uses the pole's declination of ninety

questions.explanation: Declination measures angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, so a value of +82 means 82 degrees north. The north celestial pole itself sits at +90 degrees.
questions.hint: Declination is measured from the celestial equator.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with surface temperature 11100 K peaks near what wavelength in nanometers?

options.misconception: doubles the peak wavelength
halves the peak wavelength
confuses temperature with wavelength

questions.explanation: Wien's law puts the peak near 2.9 million divided by 11100 kelvin, about 261.3 nm. Hotter blackbodies peak at shorter, bluer wavelengths.
questions.hint: Peak wavelength times temperature is roughly constant.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 8.6 m telescope observing at 550 nm has a diffraction limit in arcseconds of:

options.misconception: doubles the diffraction limit
halves the diffraction limit
multiplies back by the aperture

questions.explanation: The diffraction limit is 1.22 times wavelength over aperture, which for 8.6 m gives 0.02 arcseconds. Larger mirrors resolve finer detail because the angle shrinks with diameter.
questions.hint: Resolution improves as aperture increases.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Compute radial velocity from Doppler shift
questions.stem: A spectral line at 500 nm is shifted by 16.4 nm; the radial velocity in km/s is:

options.misconception: treats the wavelength shift itself as a speed
doubles the inferred velocity
halves the inferred velocity

questions.explanation: The Doppler relation v = c times the shift over the rest wavelength gives about 9840 km/s. A wavelength shift in nanometers is not itself a velocity.
questions.hint: Divide the shift by the rest wavelength, then multiply by light speed.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Compared with a 1 m telescope, a 42.5 m telescope gathers how many times more light?

options.misconception: uses the diameter ratio without squaring
doubles the ratio arbitrarily
halves the diameter before comparing

questions.explanation: Collecting area scales with the square of the aperture, so a 42.5 m mirror gathers about 1806 times the light of a 1 m mirror.
questions.hint: Area goes as diameter squared.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun at 8.4 AU; its orbital period in years is:

options.misconception: uses the semi-major axis as the period
doubles the orbital distance
squares instead of using the three-halves power

questions.explanation: Kepler's third law says period squared equals semi-major axis cubed, so P is a to the 3/2 power, about 24.35 years at 8.4 AU.
questions.hint: P squared equals a cubed for solar orbits.

squares the period instead
uses the square root of the period

questions.explanation: Rearranging Kepler's third law gives a equals P to the two-thirds power, about 12.08 AU for a period of 42.0 years.

questions.learningObjective: Infer central mass from an orbit
questions.stem: A moon orbits with semi-major axis 2 AU and period 9 yr; the central mass in solar masses is:

options.misconception: ignores the orbital period entirely
inverts the mass ratio
uses the period only once

questions.explanation: Newton's form gives central mass as a cubed divided by P squared in solar units, which is 0.10 here. A shorter period at the same distance implies a larger mass.
questions.hint: Mass equals a cubed over P squared.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A world with 1 Earth masses and 10 Earth radii has density about how many times Earth's?

options.misconception: forgets that volume scales with radius cubed
multiplies by radius instead of dividing
squares the radius instead of cubing it

questions.explanation: Density is mass over volume, and volume grows as radius cubed, so the ratio is 1 over 10 cubed, about 0.00. Larger worlds are not automatically denser.
questions.hint: Volume scales as radius to the third power.

options.misconception: forgets to square the radius
multiplies by radius instead of dividing
cubes the radius in the denominator

questions.explanation: Surface gravity scales as mass over radius squared, giving 0.01 times Earth's for 1 masses and 10 radii. A big radius can offset a large mass.
questions.hint: Gravity follows the inverse-square law in radius.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: The solar flux at 8.65 AU, given 1361 W/m2 at 1 AU, is about:

options.misconception: multiplies by distance instead of dividing
uses inverse distance without squaring
uses the square of distance in the numerator

questions.explanation: Flux falls as the square of distance, so at 8.65 AU it is 1361 divided by 8.65 squared, about 18 W/m2. This is why distant planets are colder.
questions.hint: Flux drops with the square of distance.

questions.stem: If fusion converts 41.5 million tonnes each second, the Sun's output is about how many times 10^26 J per second?

options.misconception: ignores the factor of c squared entirely
uses ten times the correct conversion
misplaces the decimal by one place

questions.explanation: Einstein's E equals m c squared, and a million tonnes is 10^9 kg, so 41.5 million tonnes yields about 37.35 times 10^26 J each second.
questions.hint: One million tonnes is 10^9 kilograms.

questions.stem: At 82 Gyr old, how much longer has the Sun on the main sequence?

options.misconception: overstates the elapsed time instead of the remainder
assumes the full lifetime still remains
adds the age to the total lifetime

questions.explanation: Subtracting the current age from the total main-sequence lifetime gives 10 minus 82, about -72 Gyr left before the Sun leaves the main sequence.

questions.stem: Sunlight takes about 71.4 minutes to reach a planet at 8.6 AU from the Sun:

options.misconception: uses the fixed one-AU travel time
adds distance to the travel time
multiplies by distance twice

questions.explanation: Light takes about 8.3 minutes to cross 1 AU, so at 8.6 AU the travel time is 71.4 minutes. Looking outward in space is also looking back in time.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY

omits the factor of five
uses a linear distance ratio

questions.explanation: Distance modulus equals 5 times log of distance in parsecs over 10, giving 9.60 for 830 pc. It links apparent and absolute magnitude.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with radius 1.0 solar radii and temperature 11100 K has luminosity about how many Suns?

options.misconception: ignores the temperature contribution
ignores the radius contribution
uses temperature squared instead of to the fourth

questions.explanation: Relative luminosity follows radius squared times temperature-to-the-fourth, giving 13.68 Suns. Temperature has a much stronger effect than radius.
questions.hint: Luminosity scales as R squared times T to the fourth.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with absolute magnitude 10.1 is about how many times more luminous than the Sun at 4.83?

options.misconception: uses the magnitude difference directly
multiplies by 2.512 instead of exponentiating
inverts the luminosity ratio

questions.explanation: Luminosity ratio is 2.512 raised to the Sun's magnitude minus the star's, about 0.01. Lower absolute magnitude means intrinsically brighter.
questions.hint: A difference of five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with surface temperature 11100 K belongs to which spectral class?

options.misconception: assigns a class meant for hotter stars
assigns a class meant for cooler stars
misplaces the boundary between classes

questions.explanation: The sequence O B A F G K M runs from hot to cool, and 11100 K falls in class B. Spectral class tracks surface temperature, not stellar mass directly.
questions.hint: O is hottest and M is coolest.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A main-sequence star of 8.6 solar masses has luminosity about how many Suns?

options.misconception: uses mass squared instead of the steep power
multiplies mass by the exponent
uses an exponent that is too shallow

questions.explanation: For main-sequence stars luminosity scales roughly as mass to the 3.5 power, giving 1865.3 Suns at 8.6 solar masses. Massive stars burn far brighter and shorter.
questions.hint: Luminosity rises much faster than mass.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 16.7 solar-mass star stays on the main sequence about how many Gyr?

options.misconception: uses a simple inverse of mass
assumes lifetime grows with mass
uses inverse-square instead of the steep exponent

questions.explanation: Lifetime scales as 10 Gyr times mass to the minus 2.5, which is 0.01 Gyr here. Massive stars exhaust fuel quickly despite having more of it.
questions.hint: Lifetime falls steeply as mass rises.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the fate of a white dwarf
questions.stem: A stellar remnant of 5.55 solar masses exceeds the 1.4 solar-mass limit; it will likely:

options.misconception: ignores that the mass limit has been exceeded

options.text: collapse straight into a black hole
options.misconception: confuses a thermonuclear blast with direct collapse

options.text: reignite hydrogen fusion in a shell
options.misconception: reverses the direction of stellar evolution

questions.explanation: Above about 1.4 solar masses electron degeneracy cannot support a white dwarf, so carbon ignition produces a supernova. Stable existence is impossible at 5.55 solar masses.
questions.hint: Electron degeneracy fails above 1.4 solar masses.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Match initial mass to a remnant
questions.stem: A star born with 41.5 solar masses will most likely:

options.misconception: assigns a low-mass outcome to a high-mass star
skips the neutron-star stage incorrectly
assumes the star never leaves the main sequence

questions.explanation: Initial mass decides the endpoint: under about 8 solar masses gives a white dwarf, 8 to 20 gives a neutron star, and above that a black hole. At 41.5 solar masses the corresponding remnant follows.
questions.hint: Very massive stars leave the densest remnants.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY

questions.stem: A Type Ia supernova with apparent magnitude 20.15 and absolute magnitude -19.3 lies about how many Mpc away?

halves the inferred distance
uses apparent magnitude as distance

questions.explanation: Distance modulus is m minus M, here 39.45, which converts to 7.76 Mpc. Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles because their peak luminosity is similar.
questions.hint: Distance modulus relates apparent and absolute magnitude.

doubles the Hubble constant
uses distance as recession speed

questions.explanation: Hubble's law gives recession speed as H0 times distance, about 30100 km/s at 430 Mpc. It describes the average expansion flow, not peculiar motions.

halves the inferred velocity
divides light speed by redshift

questions.explanation: At small redshift, v is approximately c times z, giving about 123000 km/s. Redshift itself has no units and is not a velocity.

doubles the redshift

multiplies by sixty instead of dividing

questions.explanation: There are 60 arcminutes in one degree, so dividing 42.0 by 60 gives 0.700 degrees. Treating arcminutes as degrees skips that conversion entirely.
questions.hint: A degree contains 60 arcminutes.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Star A at magnitude 17 outshines star B at magnitude 20 by what factor?

options.misconception: uses the magnitude difference itself as a factor
treats each magnitude as a factor of one hundred
halves the magnitude step before exponentiating

questions.explanation: A difference of 3 magnitudes corresponds to 2.512 raised to 3, about 15.85 times brighter. The magnitude difference alone is logarithmic, not a brightness ratio.
questions.hint: Each five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star has a parallax of 43.0 milliarcseconds; its distance in parsecs is:

options.misconception: mistakes the parallax angle for the distance
multiplies the angle by 1000 instead of dividing
divides by parallax twice

questions.explanation: Distance in parsecs equals 1000 divided by parallax in milliarcseconds, giving 23.26 pc. Parallax is a small angle and shrinks as the star gets farther away.
questions.hint: One parsec is the distance with one arcsecond of parallax.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star rises at 7:22 tonight; about how many minutes earlier will it rise tomorrow night?

options.misconception: confuses the 24-hour solar day with the shift
uses a full hour as the nightly advance
assumes stars rise at the same clock time

questions.explanation: A sidereal day is roughly four minutes shorter than a solar day, so a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. That is why constellations drift through the seasons.
questions.hint: The sidereal day is about 23h 56m.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: When the Moon is 221 degrees from the Sun, the illuminated fraction is about:

options.misconception: uses the wrong sign for the cosine term
takes the angle fraction as the lit fraction
forgets to halve the geometric factor

questions.explanation: The sunlit fraction of the lunar disk is (1 minus cos of the elongation) over 2, which gives 0.88 here. At full moon the elongation is 180 degrees and the fraction reaches one.
questions.hint: Full moon means an elongation of 180 degrees.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star at declination +83 degrees lies how many degrees north of the celestial equator?

options.misconception: uses the complement to the pole instead
doubles the declination value
uses the pole's declination of ninety

questions.explanation: Declination measures angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, so a value of +83 means 83 degrees north. The north celestial pole itself sits at +90 degrees.
questions.hint: Declination is measured from the celestial equator.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with surface temperature 11200 K peaks near what wavelength in nanometers?

options.misconception: doubles the peak wavelength
halves the peak wavelength
confuses temperature with wavelength

questions.explanation: Wien's law puts the peak near 2.9 million divided by 11200 kelvin, about 258.9 nm. Hotter blackbodies peak at shorter, bluer wavelengths.
questions.hint: Peak wavelength times temperature is roughly constant.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 8.7 m telescope observing at 550 nm has a diffraction limit in arcseconds of:

options.misconception: doubles the diffraction limit
halves the diffraction limit
multiplies back by the aperture

questions.explanation: The diffraction limit is 1.22 times wavelength over aperture, which for 8.7 m gives 0.02 arcseconds. Larger mirrors resolve finer detail because the angle shrinks with diameter.
questions.hint: Resolution improves as aperture increases.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Compute radial velocity from Doppler shift
questions.stem: A spectral line at 500 nm is shifted by 16.6 nm; the radial velocity in km/s is:

options.misconception: treats the wavelength shift itself as a speed
doubles the inferred velocity
halves the inferred velocity

questions.explanation: The Doppler relation v = c times the shift over the rest wavelength gives about 9960 km/s. A wavelength shift in nanometers is not itself a velocity.
questions.hint: Divide the shift by the rest wavelength, then multiply by light speed.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Compared with a 1 m telescope, a 43.0 m telescope gathers how many times more light?

options.misconception: uses the diameter ratio without squaring
doubles the ratio arbitrarily
halves the diameter before comparing

questions.explanation: Collecting area scales with the square of the aperture, so a 43.0 m mirror gathers about 1849 times the light of a 1 m mirror.
questions.hint: Area goes as diameter squared.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun at 8.5 AU; its orbital period in years is:

options.misconception: uses the semi-major axis as the period
doubles the orbital distance
squares instead of using the three-halves power

questions.explanation: Kepler's third law says period squared equals semi-major axis cubed, so P is a to the 3/2 power, about 24.78 years at 8.5 AU.
questions.hint: P squared equals a cubed for solar orbits.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.stem: A comet has an orbital period of 42.5 years; its semi-major axis in AU is:

options.misconception: uses the period itself as the distance
squares the period instead
uses the square root of the period

questions.explanation: Rearranging Kepler's third law gives a equals P to the two-thirds power, about 12.18 AU for a period of 42.5 years.
questions.hint: Take the two-thirds power of the period.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.learningObjective: Infer central mass from an orbit
questions.stem: A moon orbits with semi-major axis 3 AU and period 9 yr; the central mass in solar masses is:

options.misconception: ignores the orbital period entirely
inverts the mass ratio
uses the period only once

questions.explanation: Newton's form gives central mass as a cubed divided by P squared in solar units, which is 0.33 here. A shorter period at the same distance implies a larger mass.
questions.hint: Mass equals a cubed over P squared.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A world with 2 Earth masses and 10 Earth radii has density about how many times Earth's?

options.misconception: forgets that volume scales with radius cubed
multiplies by radius instead of dividing
squares the radius instead of cubing it

questions.explanation: Density is mass over volume, and volume grows as radius cubed, so the ratio is 2 over 10 cubed, about 0.00. Larger worlds are not automatically denser.
questions.hint: Volume scales as radius to the third power.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A world with 2 Earth masses and 10 Earth radii has surface gravity about how many times Earth's?

options.misconception: forgets to square the radius
multiplies by radius instead of dividing
cubes the radius in the denominator

questions.explanation: Surface gravity scales as mass over radius squared, giving 0.02 times Earth's for 2 masses and 10 radii. A big radius can offset a large mass.
questions.hint: Gravity follows the inverse-square law in radius.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: The solar flux at 8.75 AU, given 1361 W/m2 at 1 AU, is about:

options.misconception: multiplies by distance instead of dividing
uses inverse distance without squaring
uses the square of distance in the numerator

questions.explanation: Flux falls as the square of distance, so at 8.75 AU it is 1361 divided by 8.75 squared, about 18 W/m2. This is why distant planets are colder.
questions.hint: Flux drops with the square of distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: If fusion converts 42.0 million tonnes each second, the Sun's output is about how many times 10^26 J per second?

options.misconception: ignores the factor of c squared entirely
uses ten times the correct conversion
misplaces the decimal by one place

questions.explanation: Einstein's E equals m c squared, and a million tonnes is 10^9 kg, so 42.0 million tonnes yields about 37.80 times 10^26 J each second.
questions.hint: One million tonnes is 10^9 kilograms.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the Sun's remaining life
questions.stem: At 83 Gyr old, how much longer has the Sun on the main sequence?

options.misconception: overstates the elapsed time instead of the remainder
assumes the full lifetime still remains
adds the age to the total lifetime

questions.explanation: Subtracting the current age from the total main-sequence lifetime gives 10 minus 83, about -73 Gyr left before the Sun leaves the main sequence.
questions.hint: Remaining life is total lifetime minus current age.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Relate distance to light travel time
questions.stem: Sunlight takes about 72.2 minutes to reach a planet at 8.7 AU from the Sun:

options.misconception: uses the fixed one-AU travel time
adds distance to the travel time
multiplies by distance twice

questions.explanation: Light takes about 8.3 minutes to cross 1 AU, so at 8.7 AU the travel time is 72.2 minutes. Looking outward in space is also looking back in time.
questions.hint: One astronomical unit is about 8.3 light-minutes.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY

options.misconception: uses parsecs instead of ten-parsec reference
omits the factor of five
uses a linear distance ratio

questions.explanation: Distance modulus equals 5 times log of distance in parsecs over 10, giving 9.62 for 840 pc. It links apparent and absolute magnitude.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY

options.misconception: ignores the temperature contribution
ignores the radius contribution
uses temperature squared instead of to the fourth

questions.explanation: Relative luminosity follows radius squared times temperature-to-the-fourth, giving 31.90 Suns. Temperature has a much stronger effect than radius.
questions.hint: Luminosity scales as R squared times T to the fourth.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY

options.misconception: uses the magnitude difference directly
multiplies by 2.512 instead of exponentiating
inverts the luminosity ratio

questions.explanation: Luminosity ratio is 2.512 raised to the Sun's magnitude minus the star's, about 0.01. Lower absolute magnitude means intrinsically brighter.
questions.hint: A difference of five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

assigns a class meant for cooler stars
misplaces the boundary between classes

questions.explanation: The sequence O B A F G K M runs from hot to cool, and 11200 K falls in class B. Spectral class tracks surface temperature, not stellar mass directly.
questions.hint: O is hottest and M is coolest.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A main-sequence star of 8.7 solar masses has luminosity about how many Suns?

options.misconception: uses mass squared instead of the steep power
multiplies mass by the exponent
uses an exponent that is too shallow

questions.explanation: For main-sequence stars luminosity scales roughly as mass to the 3.5 power, giving 1942.3 Suns at 8.7 solar masses. Massive stars burn far brighter and shorter.
questions.hint: Luminosity rises much faster than mass.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 16.9 solar-mass star stays on the main sequence about how many Gyr?

options.misconception: uses a simple inverse of mass
assumes lifetime grows with mass
uses inverse-square instead of the steep exponent

questions.explanation: Lifetime scales as 10 Gyr times mass to the minus 2.5, which is 0.01 Gyr here. Massive stars exhaust fuel quickly despite having more of it.
questions.hint: Lifetime falls steeply as mass rises.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the fate of a white dwarf
questions.stem: A stellar remnant of 5.60 solar masses exceeds the 1.4 solar-mass limit; it will likely:

options.misconception: ignores that the mass limit has been exceeded

options.text: collapse straight into a black hole
options.misconception: confuses a thermonuclear blast with direct collapse

options.text: reignite hydrogen fusion in a shell
options.misconception: reverses the direction of stellar evolution

questions.explanation: Above about 1.4 solar masses electron degeneracy cannot support a white dwarf, so carbon ignition produces a supernova. Stable existence is impossible at 5.60 solar masses.
questions.hint: Electron degeneracy fails above 1.4 solar masses.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Match initial mass to a remnant
questions.stem: A star born with 42.0 solar masses will most likely:

options.misconception: assigns a low-mass outcome to a high-mass star
skips the neutron-star stage incorrectly
assumes the star never leaves the main sequence

questions.explanation: Initial mass decides the endpoint: under about 8 solar masses gives a white dwarf, 8 to 20 gives a neutron star, and above that a black hole. At 42.0 solar masses the corresponding remnant follows.
questions.hint: Very massive stars leave the densest remnants.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Find distance from a supernova magnitude
questions.stem: A Type Ia supernova with apparent magnitude 20.30 and absolute magnitude -19.3 lies about how many Mpc away?

options.misconception: doubles the inferred distance
halves the inferred distance
uses apparent magnitude as distance

questions.explanation: Distance modulus is m minus M, here 39.60, which converts to 8.32 Mpc. Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles because their peak luminosity is similar.
questions.hint: Distance modulus relates apparent and absolute magnitude.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY

options.misconception: halves the Hubble constant
doubles the Hubble constant
uses distance as recession speed

questions.explanation: Hubble's law gives recession speed as H0 times distance, about 30450 km/s at 435 Mpc. It describes the average expansion flow, not peculiar motions.
questions.hint: Velocity equals Hubble constant times distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy with redshift 0.415 has recession speed about how many km/s?

halves the inferred velocity
divides light speed by redshift

questions.explanation: At small redshift, v is approximately c times z, giving about 124500 km/s. Redshift itself has no units and is not a velocity.
questions.hint: For small z, velocity is c times z.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY

omits subtracting one
doubles the redshift

questions.explanation: Redshift is observed minus rest wavelength over rest wavelength, which is 0.348 here. Dividing by the observed wavelength gives a different, incorrect quantity.
questions.hint: Always divide the shift by the rest wavelength.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy rotating at 840 km/s at 170 kpc has mass about how many times 10^10 solar masses?

options.misconception: uses speed rather than speed squared
ignores the gravitational constant
drops the radius from the expression

questions.explanation: Balancing gravity and circular motion gives mass as v squared times radius over G, about 2789.0 times 10^10 solar masses. Flat rotation curves imply large dark halos.
questions.hint: Mass follows from v squared times r over G.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy of apparent magnitude 16.2 at 92 Mpc has absolute magnitude about:

uses apparent magnitude unchanged
uses megaparsecs where parsecs are needed

questions.explanation: Absolute magnitude is apparent magnitude minus the distance modulus, giving -18.62 for 16.2 at 92 Mpc. This removes the dimming due to distance.
questions.hint: Subtract five times log of distance in parsecs over ten.

doubles the Hubble time
drops the unit conversion constant

questions.explanation: The inverse Hubble constant sets the expansion timescale, about 11.6 Gyr for H of 84.6. The true age depends slightly on the universe's composition.
questions.hint: Age is roughly the inverse of the Hubble constant.

uses redshift directly as the scale factor
halves the redshift before inverting

questions.explanation: The scale factor relates to redshift by a equals 1 over 1 plus z, which is 0.546 here. A smaller a means the universe was more compressed.
questions.hint: One plus redshift is the inverse scale factor.

omits the one in the expansion

uses the square root of a
